Imagine my surprise when one day in 2016, while googling Jada Pinkett-Smith, did I happen across a video for a hard rock band called Wicked Wisdom? Curiosity piqued, I clicked on a YouRube video of the band performing on David Letterman to be completely shocked that this band was indeed fronted by Will Smith’s lovelier half and MIND BLOWN!

While her husband is best known for funky, pop-wrap, complete with teen angst, Pickett-Smith is growling out fierce vocals, surrounding by amazing guitarists and percussion. The songs are complex and reminiscent of Evanescence or Lacuna Coil, but have a grittier vocal than either of those bands. Her stage presence is spot on, a rock goddess, more guttural and less ethereal than Amy Lee.

The band is still making music under the name “Wicked Evolution” and their two albums can’t be found on Apple Music, which sent me to Amazon for my fix and to begin my collection. Take a listen, she even gets props from metal gods like Ozzy and Sharon Osborne. While music is indeed a matter of taste, it’s well worth the listen!

text.28:
THE ESSENTIAL BRUCE SPRINGSTEEN: It's pretty hard to dislike this three platter roundup (including one bonus disc) of Bruce Springsteen's pivotal moments...a marked improvement on Greatest Hits, which left off far too many key tracks. Somehow rockin' staples like Goin' Down, Tenth Avenue Freeze Out, and Prove It All Night all failed to make the cut here, but the bonus disc more than makes up for those omissions. Hard to find ditties...a cool cover of Viva Las Vegas, the brief but incendiary Held Up Without a Gun, and a superb live version of Jimmy Cliff's Trapped...are just a few of the welcome surprises. Elsewhere, it's mostly the expected huge hits (Born to Run, Hungry Heart, and Glory Days), tempered by deeper cuts (Thunder Road, Atlantic City, The Rising) every Bruce fan worth his dungarees knows just as well. Stark, forlorn ballads and hearty party tunes are equally effective, administered in his trademark bark, backed by the streetwise, always soulful E Street Band. Springsteen's searing, beautifully ragged axe solo on Badlands is worth the price of admission alone. Mighty moments like that one are peppered throughout Essential, which, while no substitute for definitive albums such as The River and Born in the USA, nonetheless represents the most Boss bang for your buck.

text.39:
The early 80's are probably my favorite time in music history. I've always liked the AOR format from that time between 1979 to about 1983. My teenage son, through osmosis I suppose, has become a fan of much of my music and really enjoys this same fare: Pat Benatar, Loverboy, the Cars, etc.; groups/artists that were "pop" but very COOL pop with a rock 'n' roll edge. He often laments when we listen to some of my cd's in the car, how cool it must have been to have such great music as part of my generation. He can't believe that all of this was actually played on radio and was considered "popular" because his generation is so far removed from that style.

Sorry for meandering...on with the review! For those who know Loverboy already, you may know the hits (of which there are quite a few) but if you never heard the entire "Get Lucky" album, you may not realize how good the deep cuts are. I have this on LP from "back in the day" but never owned the cd until now. When I saw it on Amazon for a ridiculously low price, I had to get it. This is one of the classic AOR albums of all time. There's no real filler on this album and the band put in fine performances. If you are unfamiliar with this album at all but are at least mildly curious about it (likely since you are here looking at the reviews), it's definitely worth purchasing at this price (under $6 at the time of this review).

I've always felt that Loverboy never got the recognition they deserved for the quality of hard rocking "pop" they produced. Paul Dean is an incredible guitarist with a keen sense of how to write catchy hooks. I think the name "Loverboy" caused many hard rockers to keep the band somewhat at arms-length; yet, I think many of those same folk secretly admired what Loverboy did on their early albums. I enjoy this slice of 80's bliss just as much as I do "Back in Black" by AC/DC or "Restless and Wild" by Accept. Great rock music is great rock music no matter how you slice it.

The early 80's produced a plethora of slick, hard rock that was dynamic and incorporated aspects of many genres. After Def Leppard and Quiet Riot showed record labels just how much money could be made via hard rock / heavy metal, the corporations began producing cookie cutter rock that was marketed for image over music. MTV didn't help either. The groups from the first years of the 80's, I've always felt, still had a dose of musical integrity and were less tarnished by corporate imaging. Billy Squire's "Don't Say No," Shooting Star's "Hang on for Your Life," Sammy Hagar's "Standing Hampton" and albums of their ilk, stand as testaments to the classic pre-digital, AOR sound. Loverboy's "Get Lucky" belongs there, too. Great music, less sullied by the extravagance of the mid to late 80's.
